lines: Provisions Point
A proposed supply and recovery shelter for Lama Lama Country.

1.2.title: Design Area and Project Opportunity
lines: Design Area: 2. Eco-tourism and Visitor Experience
Project Opportunity: 2.1 Resilient visitor infrastructure

1.3.title: How Might We statement
lines: How Might We statement: How might we make a Lama Lama Country campground safer for visitors, more resilient to floods and unreliable roads, with low capital investment and without adding more maintenance duties to Rangers, while protecting the region's cultural and ecological values?

1.4.title: Tutorial and team
lines: Tutorial 4, Team 3 (FatZCC)

2.3.title: Keywords
lines: Keywords: Visitor security, flood resilience, remote infrastructure, emergency supplies, vehicle recovery.

2.4.title: 1.2 Proposal Summary
lines: This project aims to give visitors to Warokutal (Safari Camp) access to water, supplies and vehicle recovery equipment when floods damage the roads. It proposes an elevated, minimal maintenance shelter that stocks essentials and hires out recovery kits, personal locator beacons and ultra high frequency radios.

2.5.title: Overview of design: summary
lines: The design improves flood resilience and supply security through an elevated, low-maintenance building staffed by Lama Lama Rangers during the visitor season, with a small emergency cabinet available at all times.

The implementation of this design is supported through durable, low-maintenance materials, local community partnerships to aid with stocking and maintenance, and clear signage guiding users when flooding occurs.

The building sits 2 m above ground on reinforced concrete piles, with watertight concrete walls and a corrugated fibre cement roof. It stocks drinking water, non-perishable food, firewood and first-aid supplies, and hires out vehicle recovery kits, personal locator beacons and UHF radios. A small solar system powers the lighting and charges the radios and beacons.

Visitors, Traditional Owners and Rangers travelling through Warokutal will use this facility, either during or immediately after severe floods when unsealed roads become unusable, stranding travellers without immediate access to rescue services.

2.8.title: 1.4 Key Considerations
lines: 1.41 Where the recommended materials are sourced from? (i.e. externally or locally available)

Reinforced concrete piles, watertight concrete and corrugated fibre cement sheeting, chosen for their resistance to flooding, termites, corrosion and cyclone winds. Materials will be sourced from regional suppliers and delivered during the dry season.
1.42 What are the key maintenance requirements?

Rangers restock weekly during the visitor season (July to November) and carry out two inspections a year, before and after the wet season. Hire gear is checked on return, and damaged items are repaired or replaced. Structural or electrical faults are handled by qualified contractors.
1.43 How do you propose the design might be implemented?
Community consultation with Lama Lama Traditional Owners and local land councils to finalise placement and cultural protocols.
Dry season construction by a crew of four, taking about eight weeks.
A four hour training session for Rangers, with an instruction manual kept on site.
1.44 What additional consultation/feedback/research might be required to validate your design proposal? What might the next steps be to make this idea happen?
Conduct flood-height assessments with Traditional Owners to confirm the right building height. Seek YAC approval, which takes about six months.

5.1.title: 2.1 The context of your project
lines: The primary target audience for the project consists of independent travellers and managers of local tourism facilities that operate within Lama Lama country on the Cape York Peninsula. Warokutal (Safari Camp) is a remote campground at Port Stewart, reached by roads that can become impassable in the wet season, so the national park is typically closed from 1 December to 30 June (DETSI, 2024a). The park offers remote, low-key, self-reliant visitor experiences (QPWS, 2013), but the Ranger Base is staffed only from about 8 am to 4:30 pm and campground water is non-potable (YAC, n.d.). Visitors who get stuck can be left without water, supplies or a way to call for help, which is why this project matters.

5.6.title: 2.2 Why is this important?
lines: For local tourism facility managers and rangers, the project addresses a critical operational gap. By establishing a durable supply point, the facility aims to reduce recurring emergency repair expenses and minimises the need for high-risk ranger interventions during flooding seasons’ extreme weather events. The project ultimately bridges the gap between the risks associated with tourism and wet season flooding, ensuring visitors can manage unexpected weather disruptions while safeguarding Lama Lama’s cultural and environmental assets.

5.2.title: 2.3 Which Design Area and Project Opportunity (Topic) has your group selected?
lines: This project responds to Design Area 2, Eco-tourism and Visitor Experience, and Design Opportunity 2.1, Resilient visitor infrastructure, and focuses on Warokutal. The design is an elevated, low maintenance supply point that gives stranded visitors dependable access to water, long shelf-life food, radios, PLBs and vehicle recovery equipment.

5.3.title: 2.4 What is your needs statement?
lines: The needs statement is that visitors to Warokutal need dependable access to water, supplies, recovery equipment and a way to call for help when roads are damaged, without adding to the workload of the Rangers.

6.1.title: 3.11 Lama Lama Country and its climate
lines: Lama Lama Country is located on the eastern coast of the Cape York Peninsula, Queensland. The region experiences a tropical monsoon climate that is characterised by wet and dry seasons. Between October and April, the land experiences heavy and extensive rainfall, where historical data showed that early wet season (October to December) experiences concentrated precipitation that acts as a catalyst for sudden flash flooding. This impacts unsealed roads that connect remote camping areas such as Warokutal and Maramba and isolate visitors from external emergency services.

6.2.title: 3.12 Cultural and environmental significance
lines: The landscape holds profound spiritual, historical and cultural significance for the Lama Lama Traditional Owners, who manage the region alongside the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service. Because travel through the national park and surrounding areas is restricted as it is culturally and environmentally sensitive, any infrastructure intervention must respect sacred sites and minimise ecological disruption.

6.3.title: 3.13 Maintenance and remote safety
lines: Furthermore, since regional infrastructure is traditionally maintained reactively rather than proactively, leaving remote sites vulnerable to severe weathering damage, the aim is to build something that needs to be maintained as little as possible. Currently, the Port Stewart Ranger Base serves as the primary safety outpost that is staffed, for the entire region, leaving remote camps exposed during weather emergencies.

6.4.title: 3.14 Unpredictable wet-season rainfall
lines: Rainfall in the early wet season (October to December) varies widely from year to year, which leads to flooding that is both widespread and sudden (Bureau of Meteorology, 2018).

6.5.title: 3.15 Flood damage and visitor emergencies
lines: During the rainy season, buildings and equipment are susceptible to damage from flash floods and sudden downpours, necessitating significant capital for repairs before they can be used again for tourism. For visitors, the lack of any nearby shelter or supply point makes emergencies extremely hard to manage.

6.6.title: 3.16 Existing campgrounds and safety points
lines: Camping is currently kept outside the national park boundary, at the nearby campgrounds of Warokutal and Maramba (DETSI, 2024a). There is no alternative to visitors bringing their own recovery equipment. The Ranger Base at Port Stewart is currently the only staffed safety point for the whole area.

6.7.title: 3.17 Project aims and community consultation
lines: The project aims to improve visitors’ access to essential supplies at Warokutal (Safari Camp), particularly when wet-season flooding disrupts road access. It seeks to develop an affordable, flood-resilient solution that reduces maintenance and repair demands on rangers. The design should minimise disturbance to the surrounding environment and protect culturally significant areas. Consultation with Traditional Owners should guide the design and its implementation to ensure that the proposed solution respects community need and cultural values.

7.1.title: 3.21 User needs statement
lines: User needs statement: Visitors require consistent access to essential resources, water, and safety information to manage the risks associated with remote travel, unpredictable weather, and extended stays within Lama Lama National Park.

7.2.title: 3.2 The problem and the ideal situation
lines: Warokutal (Safari Camp) is a remote campground at Port Stewart, reached by roads that can become impassable in the wet season (DETSI, 2024a). A stuck vehicle can become an emergency, because the Ranger Base has limited hours and water at the campground is non-potable (YAC, n.d.). The ideal situation is that a stranded visitor can get drinking water and supplies, hire equipment to recover the vehicle, and call for help from the campground during the open season. This must be achieved at low cost, with little Ranger work, and without disturbing cultural sites or ecological values. The design must also withstand wet-season floods with little repair, because it is unstaffed during the wet season.

8.5.title: Cultural appropriateness (weighting 3)
lines: Cultural appropriateness (weighting 3)

The design avoids culturally restricted areas, minimises disturbance to Country and is shaped by the Lama Lama Traditional Owners. Environmental impact is included here, as caring for Country covers both.
The Lama Lama people are the Traditional Owners and jointly manage the park with QPWS (QPWS, 2013), so no option proceeds without their agreement.

8.6.title: Low cost (weighting 4)
lines: Low cost (weighting 4)
The build cost must be realistic for a grant-funded project, and the facility should cover its own running costs through sales and hire income.
The build is assumed to be grant-funded and running costs paid from income (see Cost Analysis), so a design needing ongoing subsidy would fail.

8.3.title: Visitor support (weighting 5)
lines: Visitor support (weighting 5)
Visitors can get drinking water, food, first aid, vehicle recovery gear and a way to call for help in one place.
Water at the campground is non-potable (YAC, n.d.), so visitors must bring their own drinking water and supplies.

8.4.title: Feasibility and maintenance (weighting 5)
lines: Feasibility and maintenance (weighting 5)
The design can be built in one dry season and kept running through simple, scheduled upkeep by Rangers, without adding much to their workload.

Roads can become impassable in the wet season and the national park is typically closed from 1 December to 30 June (DETSI, 2024a), so the building must stand largely unattended for months and need only simple upkeep.

8.1.title: Safety and access (weighting 4)
lines: Safety and access (weighting 4)
The design lowers the risk to visitors stranded when roads become impassable, and gives them a way to recover their vehicle or call for help.
Visitors are directed to check road conditions themselves (DETSI, 2024a) and the Ranger Base is staffed only from about 8 am to 4:30 pm (YAC, n.d.), so help may be far away.

8.7.title: Community fit (weighting 4)
lines: Community fit (weighting 4)
The design suits self-reliant visitors to Warokutal and supports the way YAC and the Rangers work.
The park's management statement describes remote, low-key, self-reliant visitor experiences (QPWS, 2013), so a large or intrusive facility would not fit.

8.2.title: Flood resilience (weighting 5)
lines: Flood resilience (weighting 5)
The structure and its stock survive repeated wet seasons with little or no damage.
Roads can become impassable in the wet season (DETSI, 2024a), and repairs at a remote site are slow and costly.

8.8.title: Revenue (weighting 3)
lines: Revenue (weighting 3)
The design earns income from sales and equipment hire to help cover running costs and fund Ranger work.
Income from sales and hire reduces reliance on grants (see Cost Analysis). It is weighted lower because the main goal is visitor safety.

9.1.title: Introduction to the options
lines: The team developed three options in response to the design problem. Each was looked at in terms of what it would mean for visitors, the Lama Lama Rangers and Traditional Owners. A fourth idea, a solar-powered beacon showing river crossing conditions, was also considered. It scored lowest in the decision matrix, so it is not covered in detail here.

9.2.title: 4.11 Design option 1: Provisions Point
lines: The Provisions Point is a small, raised building that stocks drinking water, non-perishable food, first-aid supplies and vehicle recovery gear. Visitors can also hire personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios to call for help. It is aimed at visitors caught out by wet-season flooding, and it earns income through sales and hire.

This option suits Warokutal because it can be built on ground that has already been cleared. No new vegetation needs to be removed, and visitors are kept away from culturally restricted areas such as the Alingina Wungku Living Area (Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [QPWS], 2013). Its main drawbacks are cost and workload. It is the most expensive of the three options to build, and it adds a restocking task for Rangers, who already handle tourism and repairs on top of their other work (Reardon-Smith, 2023).

9.3.title: 4.12 Design option 2: Elevated tent-site platform
lines: The Elevated Tent-site Platform would raise camping areas off the ground so that tents and gear stay dry during heavy rain. It is simple and fairly cheap to build, and the raised decks handle flooding well. However, it does nothing for visitors who are stranded, as it offers no supplies, communication or vehicle recovery. Building several platforms would also spread construction across the campground, and each one would need checking by Rangers after every wet season.

9.4.title: 4.13 Design option 3: Distributed emergency checkpoint
lines: The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint would place several small stations around Warokutal, each with basic supplies, safety information and a radio, so that visitors are not relying on one central building.

Having stations in several places could mean a stranded visitor has less distance to travel for help. The downside is that each station would need its own approval to make sure it avoids culturally and environmentally sensitive areas (QPWS, 2013). Keeping several sites stocked would also add to the Rangers’ workload. The stations would be too small to hold vehicle recovery gear, and they would bring in little or no income for the community.

10.6.title: Weighting explanation
lines: The weightings reflect how much each criterion matters to the client. Visitor support, feasibility and maintenance, and flood resilience were weighted 5, because the design cannot work at a remote, flood-prone site with limited Ranger staff unless it gets these right. Cost, safety and access, and community fit were weighted 4 as core requirements from the brief. Cultural appropriateness was weighted 3 because cultural protocols were treated as a must-have, so any option that broke them would have been ruled out before scoring. Revenue was weighted 3 as a useful extra rather than the main goal. Safety is also spread across three criteria (safety and access, visitor support and flood resilience), which together make up 14 of the 33 weighting points, more than any other area.

10.3.title: Provisions Point score explanation
lines: The Provisions Point scored highest with 128 points, mainly because of its strong results for cultural appropriateness, safety and access, and revenue.

10.10.title: Distributed Emergency Checkpoint score explanation
lines: The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint came second with 104 points, held back mostly by its lack of income.

10.11.title: Elevated Tent-site Platform score explanation
lines: The Elevated Tent-site Platform came third with 95 points, as it offers little support to stranded visitors and would be harder to maintain.

10.4.title: Decision
lines: 4.25 The Provisions Point was therefore selected. It scored highest overall and offers the best mix of visitor safety, essential supplies and income for the community.

11.1.title: Detailed Design
lines: The Provisions Point is a small building of about 24 m² at Warokutal (Safari Camp), placed on already-cleared, higher ground within the campground. It is staffed by Lama Lama Rangers during the visitor season (July to November).

11.3.title: 5.1 Structure
lines: The building is raised 2 m on reinforced concrete piles so that floodwater can pass underneath. The walls are watertight concrete, which protects the steel reinforcement inside, and the roof is corrugated fibre cement, which handles heavy rain, strong sun and cyclone winds with very little upkeep. Shallow pile footings are used instead of deep trenches to limit digging on Country. A small solar panel and battery power the lighting and charge the radios and beacons, so no generator or fuel is needed.

11.4.title: 5.2 What it holds
lines: Shelves and a counter hold drinking water, canned food, firewood, first-aid supplies and safety flyers. Two vehicle recovery kits are available for hire, each with traction boards, a tyre deflation kit, a 12V compressor, and a snatch strap with shackles. Personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios can also be hired, so visitors can contact Rangers in areas with no phone reception. A small emergency cabinet stocked with water and a UHF radio is opened with a code given at check-in, so help is available even when no Ranger is on site.

11.5.title: 5.3 How it works
lines: A visitor checks in, buys supplies or hires gear, and returns it before leaving the area. Rangers restock weekly during the season and inspect the building twice a year, before and after the wet season. Sales and hire income covers running costs (see Cost Analysis).

lines: 5.31 A visitor checks in.

5.35 Rangers inspect the building twice a year, before and after the wet season.

11.10.title: 5.4 Community concerns
lines: The likely concerns and how the design addresses them:
Damage to Country: The building is on already-cleared ground, and its placement is agreed with Traditional Owners first.
Extra Ranger work: Rangers restock weekly in the season, and hire income covers running costs.
Flood damage: The building is raised 2 m, with flood heights confirmed before construction.
Unsafe wet-season travel: The park stays closed from 1 December to 30 June (DETSI, 2024a), and the building is for stranded visitors.
Misuse of hire gear: Gear is checked on return and repaired or replaced.

12.1.title: 6.1 Purpose
lines: The prototype was made to show what the Provisions Point would look like and to check that its layout works in the space available.

12.2.title: 6.2 How it was built
lines: The model was built in Blender. AI was used to generate basic shapes quickly, which were then arranged, resized and assembled into the building. The model uses the same materials as the design: reinforced concrete piles, watertight concrete walls and a corrugated fibre cement roof, on elevated ground. Each part was then measured in Blender at a 1:1 scale so it could be checked against the design.

12.3.title: 6.3 Testing approach
lines: The Blender prototype was used to check the building’s dimensions, arrangement of equipment and consistency with the proposed design and cost estimate. The checks covered floor area, raised supports, wall thickness, roof fit and storage.

12.5.title: 6.4 Floor area: prototype versus costed design
lines: The prototype footprint measured approximately 85.6 m², compared with the 24 m² building used in the cost estimate. The model therefore has approximately 3.57 times the intended floor area.

This difference means the current prototype does not demonstrate that the proposed layout fits within the costed building. The next version will use a footprint of approximately 6 m × 4 m. Its storage, counter and circulation space will then need to be checked again.

12.6.title: 6.5 Raised supports and wall dimensions
lines: The lowest column sections measured approximately 2 m, matching the dimension described in the design. The walls measured approximately 19 cm thick.
These measurements record the geometry of the digital model.

12.7.title: 6.6 Roof fit and visible gaps
lines: The roof was visually checked from all sides. It appeared to meet the walls without visible gaps in the model.
This check assessed the alignment of the modelled parts.

12.8.title: 6.7 Storage layout and equipment identification
lines: The model showed supplies placed on shelves and the counter. However, some items were difficult to identify, making it harder to compare the model with the intended equipment list.
The next version will use clearer equipment shapes and labels. Storage will also be checked again after the building is reduced to the intended 24 m² footprint.

12.4.title: 6.8 Testing findings and planned improvements
lines: The checks identified the oversized footprint as the main issue.
The next prototype will address this by reducing the footprint to approximately 6 m × 4 m and improving equipment identification.

13.1.title: 7.1 How will your solution be constructed and how will the community be trained in its construction and use?
lines: First, the project will be constructed on dry land; it will require a crew of four workers and is expected to take eight weeks to complete. Second, regarding site selection and building materials: the structure will be situated on flood-safe terrain, featuring an elevated foundation built on reinforced concrete piles, walls constructed from watertight concrete, and a roof made of corrugated fiber cement. We will also provide the rangers with a four-hour training session on how to use the facility and will leave an instructional manual inside the shelter.

13.2.title: 7.2 How will your solution be introduced to the client or community and used, constructed, managed, maintained etc. over time?
lines: First, the integration of the store will be co-designed with the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation, ensuring operations align perfectly with cultural protocols. Following this, YAC approval takes about 6 months. During operation, the ranger-operated supply and rental shelter is staffed by rangers. Rangers restock weekly, July to November. For maintenance, 2 checks are carried out by 2 rangers a year, before and after the wet season. Finally, at the end of its life: 4 workers, 1 to 2 weeks. Reuse shelves and kits. Recycle steel and roof sheets.

13.3.title: 7.3 How will the design be evaluated?
lines: Feedback will be collected periodically from tourists and residents, aiming for at least 80% satisfaction. Rental equipment will be inspected monthly, with damaged items repaired or replaced. Additionally, conditions can be evaluated before and after the rainy season, and annual expenditure and revenue can be tracked to ensure sustainable operations.

13.4.title: 7.4 How will your project affect the future workings of the client or community?
lines: The solution improves visitor safety and supports self-recovery for stranded vehicles. As a result, visitors can recover their own vehicles and access emergency supplies close by. In addition, the solution reduces ranger workload and generates community revenue. Specifically, the solution generates a reliable, passive income stream through equipment rentals; this directly funds the Lama Lama Rangers.

13.5.title: 7.5 How can the client or community take ownership of the project?
lines: The project will be handed over to the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (YAC) and Lama Lama Rangers after construction. YAC will oversee management and ensure the facility follows local cultural rules and expections, at the same time Rangers will be managing daily operations, equipment rentals, weekly restocking and some inspections regularly. Revenue from sales and rentals will cover ongoing operating costs, which allows the community to manage the project independently in the long term.

13.6.title: 7.6 How will the solution be repaired if something goes wrong?
lines: According to the established maintenance procedure, Rangers are responsible for documenting and reporting malfunctions. Damaged equipment shall be taken out of service and either repaired or replaced. Issues involving structural or electrical damage will be handled by qualified contractors. Equipment or facilities may only be returned to service once repairs have been completed and safety inspections have been conducted.

14.5.title: 8.18 Maintenance and end-of-life costs
lines: At the end of the facility's estimated 25-year lifespan, dismantling, transportation, recycling and waste disposal are expected to cost approximately $8,000, subject to contractor quotations. Reusable equipment and recyclable construction materials will be recovered wherever possible.

14.6.title: 8.12 Funding plan
lines: The project aims to secure $86,600 through government and community grants, with the remaining $786.65 funded through community contributions or fundraising. Potential funding opportunities include Queensland regional tourism and community infrastructure grant programs, subject to eligibility.

14.7.title: 8.14 Annual operating costs
lines: Annual operating costs are estimated at $3,950, covering routine inspections, cleaning, minor repairs and equipment maintenance. An additional $2,500 is allocated for replenishing supplies, although this is not included in the operating cost figures presented in the revenue projection table.

14.8.title: 8.15 Expected demand and revenue
lines: Based on the projected revenue table, the facility is expected to serve 220 visitors and provide 44 equipment rentals annually, generating approximately $8,950 in revenue. These figures are preliminary planning estimates based on expected demand during the visitor season and should be verified against actual visitor numbers and rental records.

14.9.title: 8.17 Long-term operating surplus
lines: The financial projection table estimates an annual operating surplus of $5,000, equivalent to $125,000 over 25 years under the base scenario. However, this simplified projection excludes additional restocking costs, inflation, equipment replacement and major repairs. Equipment will be inspected regularly and replaced when necessary, while maintenance budgets and rental prices will be reviewed annually to account for inflation.

14.10.title: 8.19 Financial sustainability
lines: Overall, the project shows potential for long-term financial sustainability, provided that operating costs remain controlled, visitor demand meets expectations and sufficient funds are reserved for maintenance, equipment replacement and eventual disposal.

15.1.title: Stakeholders and what is not yet checked
lines: Stakeholders: YAC (owner and decision maker), Traditional Owners, the Lama Lama Rangers, visitors, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service and Cook Shire Council.
Not yet checked: land tenure and building approval, park rules for selling goods, personal locator beacon (PLB) hire rules, and insurance and liability for hired equipment. YAC should advise on each.

15.2.title: Visitor journey
lines: Visitor journey, with the main worry at each step:
1. Plan: check road conditions and park rules. Worry: will the road be open?
2. Arrive: read the safety information, buy supplies. Worry: are there enough supplies?
3. Stuck: hire a kit and recover the vehicle. Worry: cost and time.
4. Emergency: use the PLB, or the radio if coverage is confirmed. Worry: will help come?
5. Leave: return the kit and give feedback.

15.3.title: Ranger journey
lines: Ranger journey:
1. Before the season: train and stock the shelter.
2. Each week: restock and check kits.
3. Twice a year: inspect before and after the wet season.

15.4.title: Community reaction
lines: Community reaction: The team has not yet asked YAC or Traditional Owners for their views. TEAM TO ADD: confirm this sentence is true, or add feedback received. Likely concerns are ground disturbance, extra Ranger work, visitor behaviour, theft and fire. This proposal is based on public sources and the EWB Challenge brief. It still needs to be checked with YAC and Traditional Owners.

15.5.title: Wider issues
lines: Wider issues: waste from packaging, weeds and pests carried in firewood (use commercial bagged wood and check park rules), fire risk, theft, and wildlife safety. Safety flyers should warn visitors about estuarine crocodiles and say that swimming is unsafe. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the official crocodile warning.

15.6.title: Other Considerations
lines: When introducing remote infrastructure into Lama Lama Country, community and user reactions must be carefully managed. Local stakeholders, including Traditional Owners and rangers, will need to be confident that the project respects the cultural heritage, avoids environmental degradation, and does not encourage unsafe wet season travel.

16.1.title: What should happen next
lines: 1. Co-design the building, site and rules with YAC and Traditional Owners before any ground work.
2. Complete a site survey and cultural heritage clearance for the exact location.
3. Get flood level data and an engineer's design for flood and wind loads. Confirm the roof material.

4. Confirm the rules for hiring out beacons with the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, and test UHF radio coverage between Warokutal and the Ranger Base. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the beacon rules.
5. Check grant eligibility and apply.
6. Agree Ranger workload and repair budget with YAC.
7. Run a one-season trial of kit hire from the Ranger Base to test demand before building.

16.2.title: Further research
lines: Further research: visitor counts, local flood heights, hire demand and the price visitors will accept.

Is any further research needed?

16.4.title: 10.11 Community consultation
lines: A community consultation is recommended to ensure the Lama Lama community’s requirements and expectations are properly met.

16.5.title: 10.12 Cost and funding
lines: The cost and funding should be verified, which aims to make sure the project can be fully supported on time.

16.6.title: 10.13 Regular maintenance
lines: Regular maintenance to the project is recommended due to unavoidable wear and tear of equipment, infrastructure, buildings, etc.

16.7.title: 10.14 Visitor feedback
lines: Feedback from tourists and users should be collected after the first season to find improvements.

16.8.title: 10.15 Card payments
lines: Card payment (EFTPOS) should be added, as the current lack of card payments limits income for the community.
